Data.title: Jim Cramer Announced That He Will Sell All of His Bitcoin
Data.body: CNBC’s famous host Jim Cramer announced he would sell all of his Bitcoin holdings due to concerns that quantum computers could compromise Bitcoin’s security. Cramer stated that he made this decision after an interview he had with IBM CEO Arvind Krishna on the Mad Money program the night before. Krishna had said that quantum computers could affect cryptocurrency encryption systems within 3-4 years and that investors should be “paranoid” about it. The announcement quickly spread within the crypto community. Many investors and commentators revived the “inverse Cramer” joke, recalling that Cramer’s past sell calls often coincided with market lows. Following the announcement, Bitcoin traded around $63,700, up approximately 1 percent in the last 24 hours. Related News: Billionaire Ray Dalio Explains Why He Prefers Gold Over Bitcoin The potential of quantum computers to break Bitcoin’s elliptic curve cryptography has long been debated. However, experts say that such a threat has not yet materialized in practice and that Bitcoin may transition to quantum-resistant algorithms. *This is not investment advice. Data.title: BITO: A Tactical Tool, Not A Buy-And-Hold Bitcoin ETF
Data.body: Summary I rate BITO a Sell for retail buy-and-hold investors, though it remains useful for tactical traders, options users and institutions requiring a 1940 Act vehicle. Since spot Bitcoin ETFs launched, BITO returned 21.11% versus 36.50% for IBIT, despite BITO’s distributions being included in total return. BITO’s 0.95% fee, futures-roll exposure and tracking differences should continue to weigh on long-term returns versus lower-cost spot exposure. Its 75.49% trailing yield is backward-looking and unstable, while the 0.04% SEC yield shows limited recurring portfolio income. IBIT is the stronger choice for direct Bitcoin exposure, while BTCI offers a clearer option-income strategy for investors prioritizing monthly cash flow. Introduction BITO is the first U.S. bitcoin-linked ETF and was launched in 2021. The fund’s approach allowed investors to obtain Bitcoin-linked exposure through a traditional brokerage account without holding Bitcoin directly. Everything has changed for BITO following the arrival of newer bitcoin-linked products – now investors can access Bitcoin via the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT), which holds Bitcoin directly. Income-oriented investors also have products such as the NEOS Bitcoin High Income ETF (BTCI), which explicitly uses an option-based strategy to convert bitcoin volatility into monthly cash distributions. No doubt BITO’s strategy can still participate in bitcoin rallies. I think the more relevant question is whether BITO can keep pace with cheaper and more efficient products tracking the same asset. Its recent performance suggests that it can’t, and the reasons are built into the fund’s design. I rate ProShares Bitcoin ETF ( BITO ) a Sell for retail investors with buy-and-hold approach. Nevertheless, BITO stays relevant for institutions who require a 1940 Act vehicle and also for active traders who use its liquidity and listed options. However, I think BITO’s advantages don’t compensate long-term holders for its high expense ratio (0.95%), futures-roll exposure and unstable nature of distributions. I view IBIT as the more efficient vehicle for direct bitcoin exposure. The Portfolio Adds Work Without Adding A Clear Advantage The fund doesn’t own Bitcoin directly. As of July 24, 2026, ~69% of BITO’s notional exposure came from July CME Bitcoin futures, with additional exposure through July Coinbase futures (~14%), August CME futures (~14%) and a futures-index swap (~4%). Also, BITO held ~$901 mln in a ProShares money-market ETF as collateral. ProShares BITO’s exposure creates structural dependence on the futures curve rather than on bitcoin, as it pushes the fund to continuously roll expiring futures into new ones. In contango, BITO sells cheaper expiring contracts and buys more expensive ones with a longer date, creating a persistent drag vs spot bitcoin. This can occasionally be offset by backwardation and collateral yield, but both are episodic and unreliable. Therefore, BITO remains driven by bitcoin returns, but shifting roll costs determine how much of that return BITO investors actually retain. I view such vehicle as structurally noisier and expect weaker return in a long-term vs direct spot exposure. BITO vs IBIT: A Persistent Gap Despite BITO’s 60.64% price decline, it gained 21.11% on a total-return basis since spot bitcoin ETF launched in January 2024. At the same time, IBIT returned 36.50%, leaving BITO behind. BITO’s distributions partly offset its price decline, but the fund still captured significantly less of Bitcoin’s upside vs the cheaper spot alternative. Seeking Alpha, YCharts BITO still has a chance to outperform IBIT over individual periods. In some cases backwardation may create a positive roll yield, and higher interest rates can increase collateral income. Nevertheless, this scenario doesn’t remove the longer-term problem. BITO’s distributions narrow the damage, but don’t close the gap: as of June 30, BITO reported a 75.49% trailing 12-month yield. At the same time its 30-day SEC yield was only 0.04%. The impressive headline yield didn’t compensate the weakness of fund’s strategy for shareholders. Better Alternatives Cover Both Main Use Cases Typically, investors buy a Bitcoin-linked fund for two reasons – capital appreciation or current income. BITO is no longer the best product for either purpose: Fund Strategy Annual expenses Distribution approach Best use case BITO Bitcoin futures, swaps and collateral 0.95% Distributes futures-related gains, if available Investors requiring a 1940 Act futures ETF IBIT Spot Bitcoin exposure 0.25% None Direct participation in Bitcoin’s price movement BTCI Bitcoin ETPs plus call options 0.99% Monthly option-income distributions Investors willing to cap upside for income IBIT: The Better Choice For Bitcoin Exposure As of July 30, IBIT has ~$47.7 bln in assets vs BITO’s AuM of ~$1.4 bln. BITO remains actively traded, but liquidity no longer gives it a decisive advantage. IBIT is much larger, cheaper and structurally less complicated than BITO, and closer to the return investors are trying to capture when investing in bitcoin-related funds. IBIT removes the need for investors to manage Bitcoin custody themselves, but it doesn’t eliminate custody risk as the trust’s Bitcoin is held by Coinbase. Also, IBIT isn’t registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940. Those differences may be important for some institutional mandates. BTCI: The Better Choice For Income Investors I view BTCI as a better choice for investors who are drawn to BITO’s distributions. Unlike BITO, BTCI is explicitly built as an income strategy ETF and its trade-off is clear — investors receive income, but sacrifice part of the upside in strong rallies. Seeking Alpha, YCharts Both funds have been pressured by bitcoin’s decline, but their structural differences have recently worked as intended: Since BTCI’s inception its price declined 42.03% vs a 53.76% BITO’s decline. From a total-return perspective, BTCI lost 4.40% vs BITO lost 11.50%. Thus, BTCI didn’t eliminate downside, but it preserved more value than BITO both on a price and on a total-return basis. That’s exactly what I expect from an option-income strategy in a volatile or weak market. Overall, I view BTCI as a clearer and more defensible vehicle than BITO. BITO Isn’t For Buy-And-Hold ers, But Still Has Its Narr ow Role I can’t say that BITO is totally unusable. The fund remains useful and BITO’s relevance comes from its implementation approach, not from superior long-term returns. For example, some institutions can’t hold spot bitcoin trusts but can allocate to a registered investment company. BITO gives a solution for such investors by providing a bitcoin-linked exposure within the 1940 Act framework. Another BITO’s plus is that it has an established listed-options market, what makes the fund useful for short-term positioning, hedging and options-based trading. In my opinion, BITO’s futures structure is less problematic for a trader holding the fund for short-term periods than for a long-term investor who wants to compound returns over several years. Over a short horizon, changes in bitcoin price have a bigger impact than the fund’s expenses and futures roll costs. Therefore, liquidity and ease of trading are often more important than small differences in tracking bitcoin price movements for short-term traders. Investors who prefer receiving realized futures gains as cash may also find BITO’s monthly distributions appealing. Seeking Alpha However, the issuer clearly states that distributions can vary significantly and even may be zero in some months, therefore, this isn’t a dependable income strategy. To sum up, mentioned applications keep BITO relevant. At the same time, they simply don’t make it the best choice for a retail investor seeking long-term bitcoin exposure. What Investors Should Expect Near Term I expect BITO to continue moving primarily with bitcoin over the coming months. Currently, bitcoin trades around $62,300, while Aug 2026 and Sep 2026 CME futures are ~$63,080 and ~$63,285, respectively, representing only mild contango of around 0.3% between the two contracts – that is not enough by itself to cause dramatic short-term underperformance. BITO’s collateral income may offset part of that roll cost. Therefore, if bitcoin rises sharply, BITO should also deliver a strong result and could temporarily appear competitive with spot ETFs. The weakness becomes more visible if bitcoin is flat or rises slowly. In such conditions, BITO’s expensive fee (0.95%) and implementation-related costs consume a larger share of total return. The fund’s monthly distributions may also remain unpredictable, as they depend on futures-related gains rather than a stable income source. Main near-term risk is that retail investors of BITO take almost the same bitcoin risk as IBIT or any other lower-cost spot ETF holders but receive slightly lower returns. Conclusion BITO was an effective vehicle before spot bitcoin products existed. Now it’s a more expensive and less direct route to the same underlying asset exposure. But the fund isn’t obsolete. BITO is a liquid and flexible instrument for tactical traders, options users and institutions requiring a 1940 Act structure. My “Sell” rating primarily applies to retail buy-and-hold investors, who can obtain more direct bitcoin exposure by owning IBIT at a significantly lower cost. Near-term, I expect BITO to continue participating in bitcoin’s price movements, but from a long-term perspective, its fee and futures implementation should keep it at a structural disadvantage. I expect its embedded costs to continue producing weaker returns than other more efficient bitcoin products on the market.
